speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
That, in relation to Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, not more than one further sitting day shall be allotted
to the consideration of the report stage, and two sitting days to the
consideration of the third reading stage of the bill; and
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address this very serious motion which will be welcomed by members from all sides of the House. I would not be surprised if, when the recorded vote is taken, it is a unanimous vote.
I think it is fair to say that the House will know that this particular bill has had a great deal of debate. It is one of the few legislative bills on which the members of the committee had an opportunity to travel throughout the country. The country is still talking about those travels, and just how welcome this news was. I specifically refer to my friend from Burlington who was so well received in the maritimes.
These changes, as the House and the country will know, are made to enable the government to use unemployment insurance funds for training. In the past the Liberal way of using unemployment insurance funds was just to send people a cheque. We have been training people with unemployment insurance funds for years now.
The Liberals object to this fundamental change. They would rather send people a cheque and have them kept on the unemployment insurance rolls. The way we have done it is to take them off the unemployment insurance rolls, and we have created 1.5 million jobs. Those people are now paying unemployment insurance premiums. We are going to drag the Liberal party, kicking and screaming, into the 21st century.
We think there has been ample debate in committee, and I think you will find that the amount of time required at report stage, which is a further day, is ample. There are a lot of repetitive speeches. I know my friends opposite do not like repeating themselves, but they have been. Really, we are simply saving them from themselves, from further regurgitation of Hansard.
There will be one further day at report stage, two at third reading, and this bill will go down to the Senate. I would not be surprised if it is back from the Senate in a day because that place will see it as progressive legislation, legislation which the Liberals never had the nerve to pass when they were in government. Had they done so they would have been a little better off; there would not
October 24, 1989

be so many of those Liberal hacks and flacks sitting in the Senate as appointees.
I do not intend to speak for very long today. As I sit down, let me say that the Opposition will probably want to vote on this bill immediately so I will not use up all of my 10 minutes.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just listened to the intervention made by the Minister of Justice with respect to this closure motion. I expected at least that the minister would make some attempt to justify this motion after one day of debate. All we heard was flippant, arrogant rhetoric which is the usual thing we have come to expect from this government.
Here we are once again faced with a closure motion on an extremely important bill after one day of debate. This is a measure which affects millions of Canadians. The unemployment insurance system last year paid out benefits to 2.2 million Canadians, Canadians who were obliged to claim under this program because they were put out of work against their will and needed that money
Government Orders
to pay for their groceries and rent, to send their children to school, and so on.
This is the largest social program in Canada, a $13 billion program, and the government, in this bill, is cutting and slashing at this particular program. It is cutting off debate after one day by putting in a closure motion. On October 16, a week yesterday, we spent less than four hours debating 53 amendments at the report stage. Yet, the government saw fit today to bring in this motion.
Traditionally motions of this kind were only brought in when there was evident obstruction. I challenge the government or anybody who is associated with the government to show any kind of obstruction. The Speaker himself had organized those 53 amendments into 12 groupings. In the less than four hours that we have already debated this bill we have only been able to debate the first grouping of the 12 groupings that you yourself, Mr. Speaker, had organized for debate.
I want to point out that this type of action is the action of the most cynical, the most totalitarian government that I believe we have had in this country since Confederation. This government, since 1984, has introduced closure more times than all governments since the Second World War put together.
I am willing to bet that the number of times closure has been used by this government is more than that used by all governments since Confederation. In the 23 years that I have been here, from 1965 to 1984,1 would say that closure was used maybe once or twice a year. This government uses it on almost every bill and it does it in a cynical and manipulative way. Conservatives try to make sure that Canadians do not know what is being done to them by this repressive legislation.
They put three or four very complex measures to Parliament, we carry on debate for one or two days, and then they impose closure.
This government totally misunderstands the role of Parliament in a democratic system. I venture to guess that it totally misunderstands democracy. The Conservatives believe, because they won a majority of seats in the 1988 election, that they have the right to ram through Parliament any type of measure that they please.
What they forget is that although they won the majority of seats in 1988, they did not win the majority of votes in this country. They won about 47 per cent of the votes. The combined opposition parties, the Liberals and the New Democrats, won approximately 53 per cent of

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
the votes and the government party only won a majority in two of the ten provinces of Canada. It won a majority of votes in Quebec and it won a majority of votes in Alberta. It did not win a majority in any other province. It did not win a majority on an over-all basis in terms of popular vote.
Even more important, this bill was not part of the program that the Conservatives put to the people in 1988. As a matter of fact, in the election campaign of 1988 they said exactly the opposite to what they are doing now. Time and again we have quoted the words of the hon. Minister for International Trade in St. John's, Newfoundland, who said during the election campaign in response to a question that they would not touch the unemployment insurance system, that they would not cut the unemployment insurance system, and he said that he had that confirmed from the Prime Minister.
Here we have a bill which seriously slashes the unemployment insurance system. The government itself admits that it is reducing regular benefits by $1.3 billion and that it is recirculating that money for development and for training. I will deal with that in a second. It did not put that measure to the people in 1988.
Here the Conservatives are, on this bill which does exactly the opposite of what they said in the election, imposing closure after one day of debate at the report stage. That is bad enough, but I want to recall to you, to the House and to the Canadian people that in the debate on second reading in the month of June, they imposed closure after two half-days of debate on second reading. We had one half-day of debate on Tuesday, June 6; then we had another half-day of debate on June 7; and then on June 21, they imposed closure and we had one full day of debate. At second reading, we had really two full days of debate spread over three days. That is all. Again, that was on a most important bill such as this one.
With respect to the committee, after a lot of hard driving and pushing by the opposition, we managed to get certain hearings of a legislative committee with respect to this bill. The hearings, unfortunately, were organized during the summer when a lot of private groups and a lot of voluntary organizations were on holidays, when they
found it very difficult to respond to the advertisements that were in the newspapers.
Nevertheless, the hearings went ahead after a period of organization during the summer and some briefing sessions in the early weeks of September and we had three weeks of hearings throughout the country. We had one week of hearings in Ottawa. There were four weeks of hearings. We heard from a lot of groups. We heard from 202 groups, not as many as wanted to be heard, and we did not hear a lot of expert testimony, and 157 of those 202 groups opposed the bill.
The hon. parliamentary secretary says that we should dismiss the fact that 157 groups opposed the bill because a lot of them were trade unions and they all rehashed the same brief as the Canadian Labour Congress. That is extremely misleading and once again arrogant because the different labour congresses in the different parts of the country really represent the feelings of workers in those provinces, whether it is Newfoundland, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, or Ontario.
While of course there is something in common with the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress, there were also very specific references to the type of labour force, the type of work being done, the seasonal nature of that work, and the resource base of that work from province to province. In northern Ontario, it is mining and forestry; in the west, it is resource industries again, oil, gas and so on. There was not a rehashing of the same brief over and over. They were the same basic principles, yes, but not a rehashing.
Why does this bill deserve a lot more debate? To begin with, I do not think we on this side expect that by debating this bill we are going to convince those members on the other side because they are deaf to the problems of Canadians. They do not want to hear about the problems of Canadians.
Again, I repeat, the purpose of debate in this House, particularly through the media and through television, is to inform Canadians of what is being done to them by this very harsh and cruel legislation. That is the purpose of the debate. The government is cutting off debate so that Canadians will not know what is happening to them.

They will only know maybe next year when they make a claim on unemployment insurance and find that they do not qualify. That is the purpose of the debate.
This bill cuts back and makes it more difficult to qualify for unemployment insurance. It cuts back the benefit periods. It increases the penalties without solving some of the problems that lead to quitting and unemployment insurance.
The government is totally withdrawing its contribution to the unemployment insurance fund which has been traditional, which has been in the law up until now. Last year it was $2.9 billion. The government is withdrawing that contribution and is leaving the payment of unemployment insurance totally in the hands of the workers and employers.
As a result of this bill, people will be unemployed with no unemployment insurance and they will be forced to go to the welfare systems.
In addition, by withdrawing large sums of money, a total of $1.3 billion from the fund and benefits, the government is going to be taking a lot of money out of provinces that do not have much money; for instance, Atlantic Canada and some of the western provinces. This is money that went back into those communities to help the basic economies stay alive. The government is taking that money out and we do not know where it is going.
This, Sir, will be my final remark. The government justifies the bill, as the Minister of Justice did, on the basis that it is going to shift a lot of this money into training. We on this side are 100 per cent in favour of more training, but this government cut the training budget in Canada from $2.2 billion to $1.3 billion, by 32 per cent, since it came to office in 1984. The training budget has been slashed year after year. Now the government is putting that money back into training but taking it away from unemployed workers, money that should be there to help workers pay for their groceries and their rent when they are unemployed. The government is putting that money into training and we do not know in which areas of the country.
I believe my time is up but let me repeat that this is a dictatorial, arrogant measure being imposed after one day of debate. There has been no obstruction on this bill and this is totally intolerable in a democracy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate what the last speaker just said. This is one of the most totalitarian, dictatorial things that this government has ever done. When some of the members opposite were in opposition they knew what obstruction was. They are the ones who invented obstruction in this House. For 14 days they rang the bells. When they got into power, what did they do? They limited the ability of the opposition to do the very same thing they had done. Now the opposition can ring the bells for 30 minutes. I do not know what the multiplication factor is from 14 days to 30 minutes, but I would suspect that it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 80, 90 or 100 to 1, and for the government to even imply that there has been any kind of obstruction on the part of the opposition on BUI C-21 is absolutely ridiculous and indefensible from its point of view.
What we have here is just another one of a series of cuts. The government is cutting financing for post-secondary education, cutting financing for health care and cutting VIA Rail. This is just another in a series of cuts and this time it is cutting time. I would suggest that when a government comes to a point where the only way it can defend an action-and this action is indefensible anyway-is to cut time, it shows how absolutely deprived of any kind of originality or any kind of defence it has in so far as the legislation it is proposing is concerned.
This legislation was introduced in the most glowing of terms. I am surprised, Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact, that the government did not change the colours in the Commons to red from green, irrespective of what the colours of the other House are. It is a wonder the government members did not put out the red carpet is what I am saying, Mr. Speaker, because this legislation was introduced with some of the most glowing terms that you could imagine of any legislation introduced into this House.
The Minister of Justice indicated in his opening remarks that this legislation would "drag the opposition screaming and hollering into the 20th century".

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext: You mean the 21st century.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
No, no, I think I was right. It may have been a Freudian slip but it was still right. We are getting dragged into the 20th century by this legislation, by this government. This certainly is not going to be a credit to

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
Canada or the 20th century in so far as working people anywhere in the world are concerned. This is the most devastating piece of legislation that has ever come to this House affecting Canadian workers. It has devastated a program which has been an absolute necessity to many parts of this country. In the last depression, it was able to save this country from the kind of devastation which we had experienced at the hands of another Tory government in the thirties, the Great Depression. It is because of the experience of that Great Depression that we have unemployment insurance, and it has been of immeasurable value to working people and all levels of society in Canada. There is not a merchant in this country who has not benefited since the introduction of unemployment insurance in Canada.
In many of the briefs which the committee heard as we travelled across the country, references were made to how important unemployment insurance was. The city of Sudbury was quick to point out how, when the nickel mining industry was so badly devastated because of the low sales of nickel world wide a few years ago, the unemployment insurance system was able to come to the rescue of the whole community. That is the kind of effect which the unemployment insurance has had. When the government introduced this legislation we were left with the impression that it was going to be-I do not like to use cliches but I suppose I must-the best thing since sliced bread.
To get back to what I was saying earlier, I cannot imagine why this government did not introduced it on a red carpet. But things change. The government did an impact study on what the effects of Bill C-21 would be. The government knew what the impact of Bill C-21 would be before it was introduced.
When we tried to get information on what the impact study had to say, the government would not give it to us. We went through the Access to Information Act to try to get information on what the impacts would be and we were refused access to information by this government under the law of the land through a loophole that says that if information is going to be made public within 90 days, the government does not have to release it. I don't suppose it would come as a surprise to you, Mr. Speaker, or anyone else in this country, to learn that information
was not released within 90 days. It was a couple of weeks later than that.
The impact study on Bill C-21, which was introduced in such glowing terms, was released in the middle of the summer, the deadest, dullest time, the time when Canadians have the least interest in what is going on with regard to politics, a very safe time for the government to reveal to the country what the impacts of its devastating legislation would be.
The government did not roll out a red carpet to introduce the impacts of Bill C-21. I would suggest that what the government actually did was to sweep them underneath the rug, and I do not blame the government. I do not even blame it for introducing closure on this thing. The effects of this we heard when the committee went across this land, is so bad that if I were the government I would want to get this legislation out of the public eye just as quickly as possible because it is indefensible and indescribably bad.
What are some of the effects? Let us just look at a few comparisons. The government says, even in its own impact study, that 30,000 Canadians will no longer be able to avail themselves of unemployment insurance payments after Bill C-21 goes into effect. But, as is common with this government, it has a tendency, shall we say, to underestimate the negative effects of its actions. Other studies on the number of people who will be excluded totally range from the 30,000 that the government has suggested to as high as 150,000. The people in the Avalon Peninsula, because of longer working requirements, will have to work 11 weeks to qualify rather than the 10 now required. In that area alone, 10,000 people will be completely excluded from the ability to avail themselves of unemployment insurance which, of course, certainly puts in doubt the government's total number of 30,000.
I see my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, each witness was given 30 minutes to present his or her brief. Some used the time to present a brief, others accepted questions from the committee.
The committee on Bill C-21 was under a House Order to report by October 10. The House of Commons, of course, as we can see here today, is a debating forum and the opposition put forward motions to extend the committee hearings beyond October 10 which is its right.
Throughout the hearings, and particularly during the clause-by-clause considerations, members of the opposition used stalling tactics and time-wasting manoeuvres to slow down the process.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration

speechtext:
In spite of all that, we persevered and we did report on October 10, as required in the House Order.
I approached members of the opposition-and I know they love me dearly-to see what sort of debate they wanted on report stage and third reading. I asked what sort of debate they were looking for. After all, we have had second reading, the committee has travelled across the country as agreed to by all parties, and we have heard more than 200 witnesses. We have heard from the minister and departmental officials for several hours. My questions was, more or less, "What do you want from here on?" All I got back was, "Well, I don't know, we'll have to see".
We offered at that time to extend debate during the lunch hour, if that would allow the opposition more members to express their views. Of course, there was no response. We looked at our very full agenda and the calendar and concluded that there would be little or no co-operation to conclude the debate, so we used the perfectly correct parliamentary procedure of time allocation to indicate that we intend to bring the debate on Bill C-21 at report stage and third reading to a conclusion.
In the course of debate we must make progress. If we cannot reach an agreement with the opposition parties, we have two options; we can either conclude the debate or put the bill aside for some time. We are the government and we have put forward, through the Throne Speech and other policy announcements, our intention to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. There was consultation with labour and various business groups.

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
The bill was drafted and passed by cabinet, introduced in debate, and then subjected to Canada-wide hearings, clause by clause, with the minister and her officials. The bill was finally, as I say, reported, as ordered, by October 10. Amendments were received and ruled upon by the Speaker, they were grouped for debate, and the report stage debate began.
Our task is to conclude the debate, after a reasonable amount of time. If we cannot reach an accommodation with the opposition, then we must use the rules of the House to complete each stage of debate and pass the bill along to the Senate for its consideration.
In order to show to the members that our heart is really in the right place, I move:
That the House continue to sit through the lunch hour for the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in a spirit of disappointment and sorrow at the action of this government. It is an understatement to say that this bill is unfortunate. It is unfortunate for Canadian workers, it is unfortunate for Canadian women, and it is unfortunate for Atlantic Canada. This bill is an undermining of the beliefs and sentiments that led to the creation of an employment insurance scheme in Canada.
It is a complete reversal of policy upon which Canadian workers have depended for nearly 50 years.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I suppose one has to commend the government for the provisions to bring the act in line with the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Call me a cynic, but this government's recognition of such principles comes after arduous battles before the courts for the inclusion of persons, the majority of whom are women, working for companies owned completely or largely by their spouses, and for the end of discrimination based on age. Once the courts beat them up, maybe now and again the government will act on principle.
I would also like to commend those motions before us that seek to recognize the importance of adoptive parenting, but I am proud to say also that these motions were authored by or inspired by my colleagues in the opposition.
We are limited to one day's debate-one day. What an insult to the women of Canada. This government acknowledges that the budget will increase Canada's unemployment rate. Women, as we all know, have higher rates of unemployment than men. The 1988 annual averages of unemployment were 8.3 per cent for women, as opposed to 7.4 per cent for men. Women fill over 70 per cent of part-time jobs. The majority of seasonal workers are women and immigrants. Women still face the "last hired, first fired" phenomenon.
But this government wants to limit debate on this bill to one day. Many women will no longer qualify for UI benefits. At present over 70 per cent of UI benefits are received by claimants with less than 50 weeks of work and 25 per cent by those who cannot get more than 20 weeks of work.
Women will also face, more than any other group, the brunt of the proposed double penalty for workers who quit their jobs without just cause or who decline an offer of "suitable employment". Women face more difficulties in finding jobs than many men. They change jobs more often than men because women still face a lack of opportunity for advancement, because mothers must perform the fine balancing act of matching job hours to child care hours and because sexual advances by employers may make for an impossible work situation.
October 24, 1989

The penalties are seven to twelve weeks of disqualification, rather than the current one to six, followed by benefits amounting to 50 per cent of average earnings, rather than the current 60 per cent. It is a nice message for the women and children of this country. That 50 per cent is the same rate paid in the United States. Here we go! Here comes our level playing field once again.
The government has acknowledged that it is justifiable to quit a job because of harassment, and believe me the women of Canada say thank you veiy much for this recognition of a universal fact. But it is time consuming and very difficult to prove. Although disqualification can be appealed, few women in this country have the time and the money to forgo all of their benefits and wait what could be months for a decision.
Women are often in the poorest paying jobs. They often work part time because they cannot find full-time work. Should they be trapped in poverty wages forever? I guess that is the theory of the government, to one day prevent the people of Canada from finding out exactly what is going on here, one day to prevent the people of Canada from remembering the false promises of the Minister for International Trade during the 1988 election campaign.
A recent article in the magazine, Women's Education, states: "The privatization of training as a systemic trend is detrimental to women in particular. A radical shift to funding the immediate training needs of business using taxpayers' money will not overcome the occupational segregation of women. Indeed, it may well reinforce it. Social and economic equality for women can best be promoted by the public and non-profit sectors which are concerned with the needs of the trainees and of society, not simply tomorrow's balance sheet".
That is what we have here; a bill that is concerned with tomorrow's balance sheet and probably a balance sheet that is drawn in the United States of America.
The policy and planning branch of Employment and Immigration published a study last August. It identifies the 10 occupations that will contribute most to employment growth in the 1990s; sales people, food services, secretaries, cooks, cleaners and cashiers. Need I say more?
Government Orders
The government is funnelling money from the UI account into private sector training. A study by the Canadian Association of Adult Education shows that private programs assign only 25 per cent of training programs to women-25 per cent for 52 per cent of the population.
The government failed to develop a comprehensive job strategy so it is training workers for jobs that do not exist and ghettoizing women through punitive UI measures into accepting the low pay, low skill jobs. The more things change, the more they are the same, and the less and less the cries of women in economic exigencies are heard by our friends on the other side of the House.
In its 1987 report, the sub-committee on training and employment of the Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology wrote: "The Canadian Jobs Strategy should moderate its emphasis on private sector training in regions with a poorly developed private sector".
This government is proposing the federal pull-out of the unemployment insurance system. This government is backing out and taking $2.8 billion with it. Who will take up the slack? Employees and employers will contribute more to the fund and the unemployed will pay by finding themselves ineligible for UI benefits or facing a drastic reduction in their benefits. Eight hundred million dollars will be redirected to private sector training. Will that help Lockeport, Nova Scotia? For what jobs will that workforce be trained?
I find the government's suggestion deeply offensive to Canadian workers and an affront to the principles upon which our UI system is based, principles, by the way, to which Canada is a signatory in the International Labour Organization.
When our UI system was created in 1940, it was seen as essential that the federal government should finance its share of the cost so that the system would be a national one and the federal government would assume its responsibility for economic stability and the maintenance of low levels of unemployment. Given this government's performance to date, I can see that that commitment no longer exists.
This government is wreaking havoc in the lives of Canadians. The proposed dismantling of our UI system is consistent with this government's dismantling of the

Government Orders
financial well-being of lower and middle income Canadians and the economies of the regions of Canada.
It is not the unemployment insurance system but rather the high level of unemployment which constitutes a fundamental economic problem in Canada. But maybe that truth is a little too difficult for this government to comprehend.
Hundreds of workers in my city of Halifax are facing unemployment at the hands of this government. Now it is telling them that even their UI benefits are to be cut.
This government's decision to end the At and East rail subsidy has put the Halifax grain elevator in immediate peril. Estimates by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission put the loss to Halifax by the closure of the elevator at $14.4 million. The spin-off from such a closure will further devastate the economies of Halifax and Nova Scotia.
The Maritime Farmers Council estimates that two-thirds of hog producers and one-third to one-half of the egg producers in the region will be out of business if the elevator closes. A 1988 impact study on the port of Halifax prepared for Ports Canada shows that more than 450 jobs and $13 million could be lost in the city if the elevator closes.
We are talking about the unemployment of longshoremen, stevedores, truckers, rail workers, terminal operators and all those other people who are facing the loss of their livelihood when this government begins its domino theory in the economic system of Halifax.
This government has cut vital portions of VIA Rail service. They put the maintenance centre in peril. When those Haligonians who used to have a job go to the unemployment centre, this government will be responsible. When these workers want to collect their benefits, they will be told that their eligibility has been raised from 12 to 18 weeks. So they are not eligible; or if they are they will be told they are now only eligible for 21 weeks of benefits when they used to be eligible for 28 weeks.
The government is asking the workers of Halifax to pay more for UI, to pay longer for UI and to accept less from UI should they lose their jobs. The government has
mismanaged the economy of Nova Scotia to the verge of extinction. It has mismanaged the inshore fishery by imposing drastic quotas putting hundreds of workers in the fishery out of jobs. How does it choose to make up for its own mismanagement? It imposed drastic tax measures while cutting vital subsidies such as rail service, transfer payments and now it is pulling out of UI.
The government says the onus is on private sector training, and they want the workers to pay for it. The question in Halifax and in Nova Scotia generally is: training for what jobs?
There has been a failure to develop a comprehensive job strategy. Now it plans to train workers for jobs that do not exist. I sat in on the UI hearings in Halifax. I heard a colleague from the other side of the House, who is present here today, tell the Acadian Federation to move or starve. This is not something that we appreciate in the maritimes and we will remember it for a long time.
The government has given the unemployed and soon-to-be unemployed of Halifax two options. One is to go on the over-strained social assistance. Well, we will not accept it, Mr. Speaker. The Halifax social assistance problem is facing a huge shortfall. The people of Halifax know this. The workers of Halifax know this, and they know who did it to them.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this morning to take part in the debate. A few minutes ago, I saw opposition Members objecting to a suggestion that the House continue sitting during lunch hour and that while this morning, they were criticizing the government for trying to limit- for making arrangements to have the debate go on for a few days more and then ending the debate so that we can proceed with other business. I find this attitude hard to understand. On one hand, they don't want the additional time we are giving them, but on the other hand, they object to our terminating the debate at a given time.
Mr. Speaker, during the hearings we held across this country on Bill C-21, the proposed unemployment insurance reform, we heard 202 groups during nearly four weeks of hearings. It is true that many groups
October 24, 1989

showed, if we can call it that, their opposition to the present bill.
However, Mr. Speaker, what the opposition did not say is that there was a kind of report, something you could call a work-plan, that was circulated across this country, and many groups, many unions, for all practical purposes, biased the debate by keeping the same text and only changing the figures according to local circumstances, and all this to be able to object to the bill.
We have heard all kinds of arguments, Mr. Speaker, in this debate on unemployment insurance reform. Some groups, people representing workers and unions, said it was all because of the free trade agreement and that we wanted to copy the United States. That is absolutely untrue, Mr. Speaker. There is nothing in this bill that is anything like what is happening in the United States with respect to unemployment insurance. The United States has 50 different unemployment insurance systems, while in Canada, we have one system for the whole country. In the United States, the unemployment insurance fund is about $22 billion in Canadian dollars. In Canada, the annual amount in the unemployment insurance fund is $12 billion. Considering they have 10 times our population, it should be $120 billion in the United States instead of only $22 billion.
So the two situations are entirely diffrent. We also have a number of social benefits that do not exist in the United States. Furthermore, our weekly benefits are much higher than in most American states, where benefits are much lower.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, as a result of the present unemployment insurance reform, there will be some very significant changes. Of the $1.3 billion we want to reallocate under this reform, $660 million will go to new benefits and supplementary benefits, including maternity and parental leave, which will now be far more substantial.
From now on, maternity leave will be 15 weeks, plus 10 weeks parental leave, which makes 25 weeks. This means new benefits and more maternity and parental leave.
There will also be an amendment at the report stage, Mr. Speaker, under which our government will provide five additional weeks for adoption. For instance, if the
Government Orders
child is over six months of age when he enters the home, the spouse or one of the spouses will be entitled to five additional weeks, and the same number of weeks will be added to maternity leaves when the child enters the home, after an additional period of 6 months.
So I think this is a substantial improvement that deserves to be mentioned and that will benefit Canadian families.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to the $600 million for new benefits, $800 million will be spent on training. Initially, the unions, workers, and representatives of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal party didn't want this. They didn't want us to spend $800 million on training. Gradually, however, they started to change their minds. They said: It makes sense to spend $800 million on training. We can go along with that. But this is what they want us to do, Mr. Speaker: Go ahead, add $800 million, but take it out of taxpayer's pockets. Take it out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. That is what they wanted us to do. And that, Mr. Speaker, is something Canadians cannot afford to do indefinitely. There comes a time when we have to call a halt to spending.
Canadians know that our total debt has now reached $324 billion. It costs us $100 million in daily interest. That is why today, the government is trying to act responsibly by taking the money we have and making it more productive by reallocating those funds and directing them to budget envelopes or programs that reflect our needs. And that is what we are doing under the present unemployment insurance reform.
Eight hundred million dollars will be used to train our workers. The opposition knows that, Mr. Speaker. Today, 30 per cent of Canadians drop out of high school before graduating. But what do we do with these kids? You know what happens. One or two or three years later, they are unemployed. We cannot deal with the problem, by leaving them on unemployment insurance, for weeks or even years. We have to train them, Mr. Speaker.
That is the difference between education and training. I would urge the hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundurn to listen to what I am saying. I think it is important. There is a difference between education and training. Education is when you are a full-time student at the CEGEP or university, and so forth.

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
When someone enters the labour market and then becomes unemployed because he doesn't have enough training, it is our responsibility as this country's elected representatives to try and use the money in the fund and train these workers to get them back into the labour force as soon as possible.
Look at the statistics of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. You are familiar with those statistics. In 1985, 30 per cent of the business sector said they had trouble finding qualified workers. Three years later, in 1988, we are up to 50 per cent. These figures are significant, Mr. Speaker, and that is why we want to take $1.3 billion from the fund and reallocate it to meet the current needs of a society where these people must be trained.
Regarding the new system under which people will have to work 10 to 20 weeks to be eligible for unemployment insurance, all I can say is that in Toronto, where the unemployment rate is from 3.5 to 3.7 per cent, it is a lot easier to find jobs, and it makes sense that people there should have to work longer to be eligible, compared with the situation in the maritimes, for instance, or the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region, where we see unem-ployement rates of up to 12, 13 or even 14 per cent.
I believe our reform reflects the Canadian reality, the problems in some regions and the opportunities offered in others. I think this is very sensible.
Finally, remember when in 1977, under the Liberal Government, we went from 10 to 14 weeks for a person to be eligible for unemployment insurance. That year, in the maritimes more than 70 per cent of claimants submitted new claims for unemployment insurance benefits based on the new benefit period they needed. They needed two extra weeks, and more than 70 per cent were able to produce those extra weeks! I think these figures are quite interesting and need no further comment. We are doing the same thing today. We are trying to take money that is in the fund and reallocate it to programs that better reflect our needs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was planning to have a rather pleasant lunch with an
old friend of mine at one o'clock today, but after listening to that diatribe from the hon. member opposite I am not too sure whether it will be possible to have a pleasant lunch.
As usual, that member and others on his side of the House do not address the major issue. The major issue at hand right now is what they call time allocation. It is a kind of euphemism for closure. They maintain that there is a big difference between time allocation and closure. I would submit that there is not.
When it comes to closure, what are we talking about? We are talking about chopping off a debate, lopping off your head, clapping a guillotine on your neck.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
I cannot imagine, Mr. Speaker, what the man was talking about. But let us get to the issue at hand.
No, it is true that this is not closure, not an instantaneous chopping off of debate. It is not like dropping the guillotine on your neck. But I would submit to you that there is really no difference because what really is time allocation? It is a limitation of debate. What is a limitation of debate? They choke you slowly. They strangle you slowly. They squeeze the air out of you. When it is all said and done, you are dead on the floor. So let us not talk about any subtle differences here. What they want to do is cut off debate.
What they have said to the Canadian people, particularly to the unemployed and the poor is: "Be damned, you do not count. We are not going to listen to you. We are not interested in your talk".
I remember a rather famous gentleman, who lived perhaps a little bit more than 100 years ago. His name was Vanderbilt. He said: "The public be damned!" It did
October 24, 1989

not play well then, and it is not going to play well hearing it from this bunch in this particular century.
What are they afraid of after a measly three days of debate? Is this obstruction? Hardly. So what are they afraid of? Are they afraid of a little bit of democracy wafting into the House of Commons? It would be a terrible tragedy if we heard from the people. Would it not be terrible if the public representatives could stand up and speak on their behalf? No, they do not want that. They do not want debate. They do not want consultation. What it smacks of is repression. It is totalitarianism. It is dictatorial.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, Pinochet would be proud of them. Honecker would be proud of them. There are all kinds of infamous people who would be proud. Another name that comes to mind is Noriega. You know these people have new champions, and they are over there. They do more than try to spoil lunch, they are trying to interfere with the business of the nation.
How many times have they invoked closure? In my opinion there is no difference between closure and time allocation. On this particular bill alone they have used closure twice-a dastardly action and they should be ashamed of themselves. In the free trade debate last December, they used it not once, not twice, not three, not four but five times. They used closure five times on the same bill. Is that an example of parliamentary democracy? Is that an example of responsible government? Not on your life!
I pulled the record having to do with closure. It is interesting, very interesting. In this century up until this government was elected, how many times was closure used? Was it 50 or 100 or a couple of hundred? If you measure the use of closure by this government, you probably would guess in the hundreds. But not true. According to my count, it is 23 times. Here you have a government using closure five times on one bill and twice on another. If you look through the record, you will see that in the Seventh Session of the Twelfth Parliament, 1917, it was not used one time. You can go through the list. In 1918 there was no closure, nor was there any in 1919, 1920, 1921, 1923, 1924, 1925, so it goes on.
Government Orders
Is this is a responsible government? Not on your life. The fact of the matter is though, and perhaps what is most troubling about it, is that we are not talking about some little picayune matter.
We are talking about a fundamental social program that has served Canadians well for over 40 years. We are talking about unemployment insurance. We are talking about a government that is going to decimate the program. We are talking about a government that is going to take close to $2 billion out of the fund. We are talking about a government that is going to privatize unemployment insurance. The government of the day is turning its back on the unemployment insurance program. It is turning its back on unemployed Canadians. It is turning its back on the poor of this nation. Those are the facts of the matter.
What do Canadians want? In the face of this major assault on this fundamental social program, what do Canadians want? They want to be heard. They want to be listened to. Do you think it is enough to put the committee on the road and visit 13 locations? All they received was 202 briefs. Of the 202 briefs, 157 were against it.
I met with a group just yesterday. That group pleaded with me and with the Official Opposition to give them more time and to give them a chance to explain to the country what this government is trying to do to this fundamental social program.
Is the government listening? Not at all. It is following the typical, right wing, oppressive agenda. It is all part of a pattern, part of privatization. You shut down VIA Rail. You shut down the post office. You shut down Air Canada. It all fits. Even this time allocation, this chopping off of debate, this approach of no debate and no consultation, fits as well.
For example, the government is intending to close down 14 military basis in the country. Did it consult? Did it approach anybody? Did it ask anybody? No, no, that would be beneath the government.
In closing, all I want to say is that we have a major program here which has been assaulted by the government. The government wants to cut it up and Canadians want to talk about it. They have not had the time. The government has to listen. Canadians have a long, long memory. This government thinks that a few more days of

debate is going to be a high price. Wait until the next election; the price will be much, much higher.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand in support of this motion. Every three or four years we have an election in this country. The purpose of that election is so that the Canadian people can decide who is best suited to govern them. For the second election in a row of a majority government the people of Canada said they liked the approach, the sound economic management approach being taken by this government. They elected this government to govern. That is precisely what this government and this party are going to do.
We have heard a lot of rhetoric from the other side of this House today about the guillotine, about closure, and about cutting off debate. It seems to me it was some six months ago that these proposals were first tabled in this House. We have had six months of discussion, six months of debate and talk from all sides of this House and, indeed, from one end of this country to the other. My friends talk about the lack of an opportunity to discuss this bill. I remind them that in an unusual step we went to a legislative committee which went across the country to locations suggested, I might say, by members opposite.
We have heard at tedious length what people had to say about this bill. As my hon. friend from Burlington has pointed out, time and again, we had exactly the same brief presented to us. Now we are told that there is no opportunity to speak and to discuss this bill. It seems to me that what the people of Canada want to happen is that they want to see the government govern.
We could do as my friends opposite would like. We could discuss this bill for many, many more months and then the people of Canada would say: "We elected you to govern. Are you going to govern, or are you going to talk all day?" Then members opposite would say: "Hey, look at this government. This government does not govern. It sits around and talks all day."
This government governs. This government provides an opportunity for debate. When it is clear that members opposite are not interested in getting on with the nation's business, it uses the rules that were put in place,
I might say, by the previous government which the hon. member who spoke previously now supports.
Why is it so important that we get on with this bill? It is because this bill is important to Canadians. It is part of a strategy, a strategy for the future of Canada that looks to the interest of Canadians; not one that looks back.
This government does not believe in paying people to sit home and do nothing. This government believes that Canadians are self-reliant, industrious individuals who want to prepare themselves for the 21st century. They are people who want full-time, meaningful, satisfying employment. That is why this bill is here, along with the other measures that this government has introduced.
We look to the future. We look to developing trade because through trade we have an opportunity to sell Canadian products. Through selling Canadian products, we generate wealth, economic activity and, indeed, we generate jobs for Canadians. This government does not look back. This government does not believe in building walls around the country and protecting ourselves from the world. This government believes in going out into the world and competing in the world because this government believes that Canadians are as good as any other people in this world, and we want to be a part of that.
We have confidence in Canadians. We are not afraid of Canadians and their limited ability. That is why we have put in place the Canadian Jobs Strategy along with the trade policies and the other economic policies of this government that are going to provide so much work to the benefit of this country.
That is why Canadians support this government. It is because of our sound approach to economic management. We believe that we have to have an effective unemployment insurance program as a safety net for Canadians, that the funds of that program need to be used for the benefit of Canadians.
Yet we have heard rhetoric from across the floor that Canadians are going to be disadvantaged by some of these new measures. We have heard, for example, that we should not have stiffer penalties for quitters, that this is a terrible thing. I wonder if members opposite are aware that in 1987, for example, there were over 375,000
October 24, 1989

claimants who were voluntary quitters and that this drew $1.2 billion from the unemployment insurance fund.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this government believes those funds can be more effectively utilized for the benefit of Canadians, to prepare them for the many high-tech jobs and other kinds of employment which are being created on a daily basis by this government. Over the last five years, 1.5 million new jobs have been created in Canada. That is an impressive record.
It is interesting to note, for example, that when the voluntary quitter provision was reduced from six to three weeks in 1971, within a year, two and a half times was the increase in the number of voluntary quitters. In 1976, when it was put back up again, the number of voluntary quitters dropped by one-third. The records and the facts speak for themselves.
Similarly we have heard a lot of talk about entrance requirements being increased. It is interesting to note that the experience of the previous government-and they have short memories over there, it seems-was that with the increased entrance requirements in 1977 they discovered a few years later that in fact, for example, in my own Atlantic region, 87 per cent of the people found the additional two weeks that were required to qualify.
We hear about the problem of seasonal workers, which ignores a very important provision that is in this bill. It is the removal of the repeater clause. subsubtopic: UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, October 24, marks the anniversary of the founding of the United Nations.
Some 44 years ago today, the United Nations charter was signed, launching an organization that reflects mankind's desire to "save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights, to establish conditions under which justice and respect for obligations arising from treaties -and international law can be maintained" and "to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom."
Since its inception, Canada has played an important role in the activities of the United Nations, including peacekeeping, membership expansion, and financial support of the many affiliated UN organizations such as the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, UNICEF, and the United Nations Environmental Program of which our distinguished Canadian, Maurice Strong, was the first executive director.
This year Canada attracts special international attention at the United Nations, having been voted to a two-year term on the United Nations Security Council.
We realize that the lessening of east-west tensions in our world is significant, but we cannot let this situation dull our UN initiatives to bring about total world peace and good order. We expect Canada to continue to be involved in peacekeeping efforts around the world and, complementary to this initiative, we encourage our government to take the historic opportunity and approve a comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty at a UN conference on this matter to be held in 1990.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today to pay tribute to Mr. Trevor Morgan who served as member of Parliament for St. Catharines from 1972 to 1974. Mr. Morgan passed away last week.
Active in public life for over 30 years, Trevor Morgan served as a member of Port Dalhousie Town Council, St. Catharines City Council, and the Niagara Regional Council in addition to his tenure as member of Parliament.
Trevor was always a passionate advocate for his constituents' interests. A degenerative eye disease claimed his eyesight in the 1960s but Mr. Morgan continued his career despite his disability. He was a lawyer who was a fierce adversary in the courtroom. This is a fact to which I can personally attest.
The people of St. Catharines will miss Trevor Morgan. I wish to express their deepest sympathies to his wife, Linda, and son, Graham Trevor.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising under the provisions of Standing Order 31 to express my outrage that another major Canadian plant has become a victim of the infamous free trade agreement.
This morning Fibreglas Canada announced reductions in its Canadian operations over the next several months. The majority of the 371 employees at the Sarnia plant will be affected by the plan and will leave the company in the second quarter of 1990. This is the second announced
lay-off in the Samia-Lambton region that will impact on these dedicated employees, many of whom have lived in my constituency for many years and face a bleak winter of uncertainty.
The so-called rationalization of industry, brought about by the free trade agreement, has resulted in a host of mergers and a continuing exodus of jobs to the United States.
I ask the government today to intercede and stop this merger mania, re-examine the free trade agreement, and bring in a fair trade agreement which will protect Canadian workers, Canadian farmers, and stop the plundering of our resources.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem that the Conservative Government has not lost its bad habits. We learned from our candidate in the by-election to be held in Chambly, Phil Edmonston, that the Minister of the Environment is getting read to go to the riding of Chambly next Saturday to announce another election goody, a big subsidy for the local community television station, a subsidy which the New Democratic candidate has been requesting for a long time now.
The Conservatives are not looking after the people in the riding of Chambly. They have not yet replaced their corrupt, convicted Member and they are still delaying keeping their promise to Saint-Basile to compensate for the damage caused by the PCB fire.
Mr. Speaker, when will they announce another subsidy for the Desjardins Movement to compensate for the $20 million that institution says it will lose with the GST? Mr. Speaker, it is high time for Chambly to have a real member of Parliament and that should be Phil Edmonston, an honest New Democrat of integrity!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to salute the men and women of Canada who have embraced the spirit of entrepreneurship and have started some 750 small busi-
October 24, 1989

nesses across the country since 1984. With this in mind, two important addenda are worth mentioning.
First, these businesses have proven to be resilient. Over the past decade, more than three-quarters of all new businesses survived the crucial first year of operation. Second, between 1980 and 1985, female entrepreneurs represented more than half of these owner operated business start-ups.
We as a government recognize without hesitation that small business is the backbone of our economy. It is the greatest source of new ideas, new opportunities, new wealth, and new employment. Between 1978 and 1987, the small business sector accounted for more 80 per cent of all the net new jobs created in Canada.
Nowhere has the contribution of small business been more evident than in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton. We have been a community very reliant upon the cyclical nature of one industry, the petrochemical refining industry. Yet today, primarily through the initiatives of local men and women, small businesses have diversified the local economic base and effectively lowered the unemployment rate from an historical high in 1984 to one that is lower today than the provincial average.
In the spirit of Small Business Week, I pay tribute to both the present and the future entrepreneurs of Sarnia-Lambton and across this country.

Mr. Speaker, after months of lobbying the Bourassa government, the efforts of Quebec's prospectors have finally paid off. The Minister of Finance of Quebec has just announced that the flow-through shares program will be improved.
Since last year, half the deduction for mining exploration expenses is allowed in calculating the cumulative net investment loss (CNIL).
Quebec Mines Minister Raymond Savoie had to make an extra effort to convince his leader Robert Bourassa and his finance minister.
For two years, Quebec's mining regions like Abitibi-Temiscamingue have been very concerned about their economy. Many junior mines have had to close while
they wait for better days. In Abitibi-Temiscamingue, unemployment has risen significantly.
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada must follow Quebec's example and also agree to eliminate CNIL on half the federal deduction for the purchase of flowthrough shares.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-41 is about telecommunications. It implements the approach of the Supreme Court confirming that we have one national telecommunication telephone network that crosses provincial boundaries and clearly falls under federal authority. Its aim is to resolve the jurisdictional confusion which presently exists and to allow for a simplified regulatory framework. It is not a bill that is to set local or long distance rates. That is the mandate of the CRTC, the regulator.
The Supreme Court's ruling does not mean that western and other provincial voices will be ignored.
The minister could have deposited a more comprehensive bill, avoided the serious concerns being raised, recognized the history of social responsibility by provinces, and included the means for provincial participation on local questions of telephone service.
To alleviate concerns, first, the minister must go on record in support of universal affordable telephone service. Second, he should assure Canadians that the current situation with regard to independent telephone companies is not intended to favour any one region of Canada over any other. Third, he should reaffirm the federal jurisdiction and that it does not mean higher local telephone rates.

Mr. Speaker, in light of this being Small Business Week, I want to congratulate the Colchester, Truro, Stewiacke regional economic development task force for its initiative in planning an intermodal transport terminal and lifestyle business park for Debert, Nova Scotia.

October 24, 1989
To bring this project to a successful conclusion will require co-operation from all levels of government and industry including several federal departments and CN.
I urge all ministers involved to assist in all manner possible to ensure completion of this much needed intermodal park to service the area and encourage much needed employment.

Mr. Speaker, next week the House of Commons Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs begins public hearings into the operations of Canada Post. The committee will, among other things, learn how Canada Post management decisions are affecting the delivery of postal services to rural Canada.
In the meantime, Canada Post is continuing to convert and close post offices in small and medium sized communities despite public opposition.
A report from the previous standing committee called the actions of Canada Post heavy-handed but was ignored by both the corporation and the minister.
I call upon the minister responsible for Canada Post to show respect for the people of rural Canada and place a moratorium on all post office conversions and closures until the standing committee has completed its hearings, issued its report, and Parliament has had time to respond to its recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, under the auspices of the Arms Control Centre, Canadians are hosting the Canada-Soviet Conference on Canadian-Soviet Arctic Co-operation. Discussions and panellists so far have driven home the absence of Canadian policy with respect to the Arctic and to Arctic issues.
That is bad enough, but what is worse is the government's spokesmen have poured cold water on initiatives presented in a report by the panel on Arctic arms control that recommended among other things the establishment of a central Arctic demilitarized zone, a conference
on Arctic security and co-operation, and the creation of an ambassador for circumpolar regions.
The government do-nothing vacillation is not a viable response to Soviet invitations for discussion and reciprocal co-operation in the region, nor is it a serious response to initiatives by expertise in the field.
I call on the government to examine thoroughly, thoughtfully, and with openness, the recommendations made by the panel on Arctic arms control and then to respond positively to invitations for peace.

Mr. Speaker, the essence of the tabling of the annual Report of the Auditor General, the subsequent public scrutiny, and the follow up work has improved accountability to ensure that taxpayers' dollars are spent prudently.
This year the Auditor General tells us of real progress made in following up recommendations of previous years. His report indicates a notable improvement in accountability.
In regard to the control and accountability of Crown corporations, the Auditor General notes that our own observations support the view that vigilance and stability have characterized the Crown corporation sector in recent years. He continues:
-the framework set out in legislation is not solely responsible for the
demonstrated improvements. Strong and sustained attention by all
concerned has played an important part in making this system work.
We have not yet reached perfection, but there is no question that government today is more open and more accountable than at any time before in our history.

Mr. Speaker, nearly 60,000 men and women who have lost their jobs due to the free trade deal are asking who benefited from the deal. As a matter of fact, most Canadians are asking who benefited from this free trade deal. Today we find out.
October 24, 1989

Mr. Allan Gotlieb, Canada's ambassador to the United States for the past seven years, is becoming an adviser to the Philadelphia law firm of Pepper, Hamilton and Scheetz. Since he helped negotiate the free trade deal and knows all of the elements of the free trade deal, his job will be to advise the Americans on how to take advantage of the free trade deal, probably at the expense of Canada.
When Canadians are wondering who benefited from the free trade deal, Allan Gotlieb can say: "I personally have benefited".

Mr. Speaker, today, on October 24, United Nations Day, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the anniversary of the founding of the United Nations Organization which is now 44 years old.
The UN officially became an organization on Octob-ber 24, 1945, a successor to the League of Nations created by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. That day marked the beginnings of an organization that reflected the hopes of the peoples of this world and their determination to maintain international peace and security; to achieve international co-operation in solving problems of an economic, social and cultural nature; to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war; to affirm their faith in fundamental human rights; and to promote social progress and better standards of living in larger freedom. That is the ultimate goal of the UN.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the recipient of the 1989 Pearson Medal for Peace, Maurice Strong, who received the award for his personal and volunteer efforts.

Mr. Speaker, the number one concern in Canada at the
moment is the environment. Although the government has repeatedly claimed that this issue is at the top of its list of priorities, it has done very little to back up these claims.
The government is now being given the opportunity to do something positive about the environment by providing the expertise and financial commitment needed to extend a natural gas pipeline into the province of New Brunswick.

This project will enable the province to stop using coal, a source of acid rain, which is now being used in the thermal power stations that produce the province's electric power. Natural gas could also be used by large plants such as pulp and paper mills.
Mr. Speaker, if the federal Government is really serious about the environment, it should take steps as soon as possible to give the province and the companies concerned all the help they need to bring this project to fruition.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a unique process now being developed by a local company named B.C. Chemicals, in Prince George, British Columbia.
With the assistance of both federal and provincial governments, pulp and industry waste tall oil, which is now being burnt, will be recycled to produce value added products such as resins, adhesives and stains. It can also be used to reprocess asphalt. Indeed, I am proud to say that this product is now being tested near Quesnel in my riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin. This is a good example of environmental awareness combined with good business sense.
My hat is off to western economic diversification, the Department of Forestry, the Province of British Columbia, and especially B. C. Chemicals for a fine example of western initiative.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the opposition of a few facts. The labour force development strategy tabled in April, 1989, made clear that the UI system was going to be improved. We travelled from Vancouver, British Columbia, to St. John's, Newfoundland. We stopped in every province of Canada. We heard witnesses in every province. We heard witness for three weeks in Vancouver, British Columbia; Edmonton, Alberta; Saskatoon, Saskatchewan and Winnipeg, Manitoba. In Ontario the committee held hearings in Toronto and Sudbury. In Quebec, the same committee held hearings in Montreal and Jonquiere. In New Brunswick, the committee sat in Moncton. Because we were not able to go to the territories, representatives of the territories were invited to come to some of the provinces. We heard the minister and her officials. We studied the bill clause by clause. Last week, we began the report stage.
We are debating a motion to allocate time for further consideration of Bill C-21. Members opposite say they were not given enough time for consideration of this bill. As I have just explained, this bill has been under consideration since June, 1989, and the policies underlying it two months before that.
What is the opposition doing now? Today opposition members turned down the opportunity to sit through lunch. Last week, on the first day of report stage, they turned down the opportunity to sit through lunch. They wanted nothing to do with the idea of extended hours.
Recently, one of the senior members of the New Democratic Party was quoted in a Toronto newspaper as saying that his party would refuse to agree to the scheduling of House time for the remaining stages of Bill C-21. It could not be more evident that opposition claims of shutting off debate are unfounded.

Mr. Speaker, we are in the first stages of a national plan to achieve a fundamental economic goal, which is to use our human resources more wisely. This plan became official last April, when the Minister of Employment and Immigration outlined the new labour force development strategy, a set of measures to make our country more competitive by improving the way it uses the skills and energies of Canadians.
So far, the Canadian labour market has failed to deploy sufficient efforts to upgrade human resources. The new strategy is therefore a battle against waste, and to wage this battle, we intend to use, through Bill C-21, the resources of our unemployment insurance system and make it a tool for training and development.
Waste occurs at practically all levels in the labour market, including entrance levels. Too many young Canadians lack the necessary basic skills to obtain their first job, while the national average drop out rate is 30 per cent. We are about to enter the 90s, a decade during which, according to all the forecasts, most new jobs will require a grade 12 education.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the areas of education and training are complex and are dependent on provincial governments, regional labour market requirements and constantly changing qualifications. The government is not the sole agency responsible for training a highly qualified and educated labour force, but it can act as a catalyst. Thanks to the labour force development strategy, we now have a framework for co-operation that will be able to draw on the contributions of educators, the provinces, unions, employers and all Canadians, as never before.
Within the framework of this strategy, we are adding $100 million for training new workers, to the $485.4 million we are already spending in this area at the present time.
These measures, and others in which the private sector will play a major role, are aimed at improving our competitive position generally, but we will not succeed as long as Canadians are unable to find work because they lack the requisite skills.
Under Section 26 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, we can provide training for people who are unemployed. At the present time, we are spending only $350 million of the $13 billion in the UI fund on this option. We intend to raise this amount to $700 million. In this case, plans provide for direct participation by business and unions in promoting and managing training programs. We intend to support and facilitate their activities in this respect.
We also intend to spend $150 million on programs for people who find it particularly difficult to re-enter the labour market, including welfare recipients and older workers who are 45 or over.
Mr. Speaker, speaking of older workers, I would like to address another measure that seems particularly relevant in Canada today. Any program or practice aimed at preventing a Canadian who is able to work from doing so only because of his age is a waste of manpower. And that is the case with our system present UI system.
As soon as Canadians reach the age of 65, whatever their skills or ambitions may be, they fall into a trap: they no longer have the right to contribute to the unemployment insurance plan or receive benefits. The changes we

Government Orders
are proposing will also entitle older Canadians to unemployment insurance benefits as long as they wish to work.
This measure, Mr. Speaker, and other measures provided under Bill C-21 will make it possible to take a new and intelligent approach to unemployment insurance, an approach that will make the system more relevant and will provide for an increased focus on training, a focus that is well overdue.
