Those are the words of the government's former Deputy Prime Minister, a former colleague. He would be ashamed, thoroughly ashamed, to witness the spectacle that is going on on the other side of this House today. His book, that great litany of delight, which has such a wonderful appendix in it, is something I would commend for reading to hon. members opposite. They might find it helpful, as they review their future careers in this House, to look at their past record as assessed by the former Deputy Prime Minister.
Having looked at what he said, how can this government square what it is doing today with the example set by Mr. Nielsen and, indeed, by all their leaders in the past? The use of closure by this government has exceeded all past known records. Never has a Parliament in Canadian history had closure applied as frequently as this Parliament has done already, and we have only been sitting for 10 or 11 months, in theory, but in practice the sittings have been much less than that.
Let us review the number of times it has been used. Last December the government used it to suspend the rules of the House so it could ram through the free trade bill. Then the Tories used it three times on the free trade bill, the first time since 1956 that closure had been so abused. It is a shocking example. Three times it was used on that bill. They got it through in the minimum amount of time in this House by using closure at every stage at the earliest possible opportunity.
You would think that having done it once, the Conservative members would give up and say: "Okay, we have abused our position, perhaps, once. We had some justification in the previous Parliament." But let us look at the record.
The government called us back after three months off; January, February and March. We were called back for April, May and June, and by June the government was using closure again, because it said we were not passing its bills quickly enough.
If the bills are not going through fast enough to satisfy this bunch, I suggest they should have had us here in January, February and March when we could have discussed them. But government members said, "No, we don't need Parliament around. Parliament is something we don't want to hear from. Parliament damages our reputation. Parliament tarnishes the reputation of this government in the eyes of the public because they see how bad we are." That is their attitude and they should think that way because they are dreadful. This bill is dreadful and I will deal with its merits in a moment.
That is not all. We had closure applied three times in June; on the bill on plant breeders' rights, on this bill at second reading and on the excise tax amendment. Then we had notice given on Bill C-36 in October. We had notice given on the income tax bill, Bill C-28, the other day. Now we have a gagging order, under a different rule admittedly, but a gagging order. This is the first time this has been used in our Parliament but it is the same
October 24, 1989

principle. It is an attempt to gag debate, to throttle the rights of this House to have open and free discussion of the government's legislative proposals. I say to the ministers opposite that they should be ashamed.
Let's look at the record of this bill itself. The bill was read for the first time on June 1 of this year. It was debated at second reading on June 6, and again on June 7 and June 21. Let's see how long it was discussed on each of those occasions. On June 6 it was discussed one hour and 40 minutes. On June 7, two hours and 40 minutes; and on June 21, the day the government applied closure at the second reading stage, nine hours and one minute.
That is the total length of time spent on second reading. The Tories rammed the bill through at second reading and then they adjourned the House for the summer. That is how urgent they regarded this thing. They said, "Oh well, we can adjourn the House for an extra two weeks in September because we don't need to have everybody back on this. It is not urgent." Now, all of a sudden it is urgent, they have to have this bill through tomorrow.
We have had only one day of debate at report stage. Look at the Order Paper. There are 43 amendments set down to discuss at report stage on this bill. Obviously it is highly contentious. As well are a lot of problems with this bill. Every speaker has said so. The government closes its ears and says, "We are not going to listen to that. We don't want the Canadian people to hear that. We are going to cut off debate in this House so they can't hear it." It is a disgraceful way to run a Parliament.
The responsibility for running this House rests over there. It is the government that controls the agenda in here. Everyone knows that, and it is ramming the bill through this House and not giving the members of the opposition a decent opportunity to make the points that they should be making against this dreadful bill.
Let me turn to some of the comments that have been made about Bill C-21. This Unemployment Insurance Act affects one of the premier social programs in Canada. It is a huge expense, about $13 billion as I
Government Orders
understand it. That is a very significant social program in Canada and these changes are significant. They are major changes. They have been denounced by almost every group who appeared before the committee condemning these changes. Yet this government sits here and says, "We don't want to discuss it any more. One day in committee stage is more than enough. Canadians are hearing too many bad things about our policies. We don't want to discuss it any more."
Listen to what the Canadian Council on Social Development had to say about Bill C-21. Let's listen to some of the criticism it has made of this bill and see why the government is so reluctant to have it discussed. I think these reasons betray the justification that the government claims for using closure. It indicates that the government does not want to hear these criticisms. Let me read some of them into the record.
In a recent communique released October 2, subsequent to its presentation to the committee, the Canadian Council on Social Development said this:
Low-income workers will be disproportionately affected by the cutbacks: 80 per cent of those affected will have incomes under $25,000 a year, according to calculations by Global Economics Ltd.
The main disincentive to work is not UI benefits, but low wages. Most jobs available to UI recipients are at, or scarcely above, the minimum wage. A worker making the $4.00 federal minimum wage today, earns an annual income of $8,320. The average provincial minimum wage in 1986 supported a worker with dependent spouse and child at only 48 per cent of the Statistics Canada poverty line. The solution is to improve wages, not lower UI benefits.
The proposed financing arrangements are regressive. Low income workers pay a larger percentage of their total earnings into UI premiums than do higher-income workers. Likewise, smaller employers pay proportionately more than do large employers. By funding labour adjustment programs from changes to UI, the government is shifting the burden from general taxation onto employers and workers, and more so onto those at lower income levels. Since a two-earner family with two children living on $20,000 a year will-as a result of this government's policies-be paying $1,424 more in income and sales tax in 1990 than in 1984 (according to CCSD calculations), low-income Canadians can ill afford the further burden of UI changes.
That is the statement by the respected Canadian Council on Social Development. Those are the criticisms that it levels against this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand in support of this motion and I welcome this opportunity to speak.
This government wants to get this wonderful country operating with every worker in a place of meaningful employment. It is urgent that no time be lost. Bill C-21 will help women, youth, part-time and seasonal workers, disabled and aboriginal peoples, older people and unemployed to take advantage of programs that will enhance their ability to take their place in the workforce. It will open the doors to better quality jobs and higher wages.
We have been accused of being hard-hearted, cold, uncaring and unloving, but let me tell you, we are just the opposite. This government believes in giving Canadians the opportunity to train and retrain for jobs that are waiting to be filled. How much better to be working than sitting with unemployment benefits and no hope. Remember, we are the government which has created the opportunities that increased jobs since 1984 by 1,555,000. Statistics Canada has said that since January we have created 189,000 jobs.
I just want to mention here that the unemployment insurance program is vital to the well-being of Canadians. Its role as a social safety net in providing temporary income protection to unemployed Canadian workers is essential and it is endorsed by this government.
A recent survey by Statistics Canada showed that 14 per cent of Canadian manufacturers were facing production problems due to a lack of skilled labour. Unless action is taken, these problems will likely become more acute in the 1990s.
Bill C-21 is a strategy for the future of Canada. It is one of many policies which have been developed to turn this country from being debt ridden to a country of sound management. We must not delay this program. Let us get on with the jobs we have been elected to do and support this motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address this motion of the government. I have been in this House now for five years. Over the course of the last five years this government, in an ever-more-frequent fashion, has invoked closure in order to cut off and stifle debate on issues of national concern.
We have before us a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, a bill that will affect, in a very direct way, hundreds of thousands of Canadians, a bill that will adversely affect the working poor in Canada. This government, in its arrogance, has decided to invoke closure to cut off debate.
You, Sir, have considerable experience in this House. You have been here for quite a number of years and know the rules of parliamentary procedure with respect to the invocation of closure and the stifling of debate. Yes, there is a place for closure in a democratic system. At times it may be necessary for a government, in very extreme circumstances, to cut off debate, to eliminate further discussion of a piece of legislation. But I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that those situations are extremely rare indeed. This government has done an about-face.
A few years ago when the Conservative party was in opposition its members spoke about the arrogance of closure. They referred to it as repugnant. The former Deputy Prime Minister, Erik Nielsen, on many occasions stood up on this side of the House when he was in opposition and criticized the imposition of closure. In fact, ministers of the Crown in the House here today have stood up and spoken against the bringing in of closure.
October 24, 1989

I think it is important that we ask why this government has decided to cut off debate, to muzzle discussion of this particular piece of legislation. I think the reasons are obvious. Of the 202 groups that appeared before the committee, the overwhelming majority opposed this bill. The overwhelming majority, 157 to be exact, recommended some very major changes.
It is not as if this is the first time that this government has brought in closure with respect to Bill C-21. In fact, at second reading stage, closure was invoked and, as was indicated previously, this bill was debated for a total of about 12 or 13 hours. That is not a long period of time when you consider the ramifications of the provisions in this particular bill.
Finally the bill did go to committee. The committee did travel. It did listen to Canadians. The itinerary was not as extensive as the opposition wanted it to be.

speechtext: It was exactly what the opposition asked for.

But the committee began to deliberate on some of the recommendations that were made by the various groups that appeared before the committee. Instead of debating fully the recommendations and amendments presented by the opposition, for the second time in the consideration of Bill C-21 at committee the Conservative members again invoked closure to cut off further debate.
Here we are back in the House at report stage and this government again invokes closure. It is clear why it is doing so; it is clearly embarrassed. The government knows that the longer we debate and discuss this particular legislation, the more opportunity Canadians will have to respond and the more heat it will take for this very regressive measure.
It is not as if the parliamentary timetable would not permit some extra discussion and debate on the 43 amendments that are on the Order Paper and before Parliament. The Prime Minister decided in June that he would take a three or four-month holiday, notwithstanding that the rules of the House specified a specific period of time for this House not to be in session. This government decided to take a few extra weeks' holiday, much to the chagrin and opposition of members on this
Government Orders
side of the House. Why, if the government was so intent on dealing with this bill in such a quick fashion, did it not recall the House at an earlier point in time? Why, for example, has the House leader for the Conservative party not asked the opposition House leaders to extend the debate into the evening hours? It is clear that this government does not want any further discussion or debate.
The invocation of closure goes contrary to some of the very basic tenets of democracy, of the parliamentary system of government. In any democracy it is important that governments introduce legislation , that there be a fair and full debate and that the opposition be permitted to present alternatives. In the end, the government has a sufficient number of members in order to defeat any proposal made by the opposition parties.
What is important in a democratic system is that there be that debate, that discussion, in order for Canadians to fully understand. To invoke closure, in my respectful submission, Your Honour, is to show contempt for this Parliament. Contempt has been shown not only on this occasion but on many other occasions in the past five years, including in the past year or so, when this government on numerous occasions-four times during the free trade debate-invoked closure.
Canadians believe that there ought to be discussion and debate and will not accept arrogance on the part of the government. We in the opposition would very much like the opportunity to debate the merits of Bill C-21. A great number of my constituents will be directly affected by the provisions of this piece of legislation that runs about 33 pages.
I believe that I have a responsibility, indeed a duty, to speak to this bill, to articulate in the House of Commons and at committee how this particular legislation will affect my constituents. Because this government has chosen to invoke closure, my parliamentary privileges are affected in an adverse way because I will not have that opportunity to present my objections to Bill C-21.1 will not have the opportunity to share with my colleagues on this side of the House and on that side of the House the reasons why the constituents of York South-Weston will be adversely affected by this piece of legislation.

Government Orders
In summary, let me say that we on this side of the House do not accept the arrogance of this government. We want to continue to debate this bill to discuss the merits of the legislation.
I know that I have but a few minutes to put on the record some of the concerns that I have. You are indicating, Mr. Speaker, a minute. Now how can I, in one minute, in 60 seconds, deal adequately with a bill that has 33 clauses, a bill that has drawn the attention of over 200 groups? How can I, in a reasonable fashion, deal with this bill in 60 seconds?

speechtext: It's impossible.

I challenge other members of long standing in this House to point to another government at any point in history that has shown the arrogance and the undemocratic nature that this Conservative government has shown. You sitting in the chair, Mr. Speaker, should not allow that to happen. I would ask you, Sir, to stand up for those rights.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot stress how important the passage of this bill is to the agricultural industry of Canada. Farmers have made economic decisions based on the availability of advance grain payments; agri-business is relying on farmers making economic decisions whether it be in the area of purchasing equipment, fertilizers or seed; rural municipalities are expecting that taxes will be paid. Canadians generally have come to depend on this traditional availability of cash, and to delay Bill C-36 any further would be a disservice to those whose employment and standard of living depend on this bill. To delay is purely unconscionable.
This bill is important to farmers. They have told me that they are prepared to pay their share of the national debt. There is absolutely no argument with them in any way, shape or form on that subject. However they do object to members of the opposition delaying this bill, and they have said that they will remember them next

election day. They have said to me: "You are the government; you fix this matter." Therefore I move:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in direct response to the motion put forward by the hon. member for Regina-Wascana, he must have the interests of Saskatchewan producers at heart. He must know that this bill, as it stands today, cannot go forward without proper and adequate debate in the House. It is particularly within the knowledge of the government and the government member who moved this motion that the Advance Payments for Crops Act, up until this point, very clearly outlined that this bill provided for the easy sale of grains and for the orderly marketing of grains under the Canadian Wheat Board.
It is not a loan that the farmer borrows against the crop that is in the bin. It should not be subject to the payment of interest, and that is essentially the nature of the bill before us.
The government is insisting that farmers pay an interest rate on the loan. Let me read into the record something that was in the local newspaper in my riding to support the argument that I am making here. The Prairie Pools was quoted in the North Battleford News Optimist as calling for a reinstatement of the interest-free cash advance for farmers. In a letter to the agriculture minister, which the Minister of Agriculture must have received by now, the president of Prairie Pools, Mr. Doug Livingstone, stated: "the interest-free cash advance is valuable in providing farmers with much needed cash during surplus stocks and tight quotas". Let me quote directly from that letter. Mr. Livingstone states: "Charging interest on cash advances may affect a producer's ability to wait for delivery opportunities later in the year".
Government Orders
The Prairie Pools and other farm organizations across the prairies have been telling this government since April 27, when this government first announced that it was going to go ahead with this bill, that this is not a program that should be subject to interest rates. This is quite clearly a program that allows for the sale of farm products.
I am sure you have seen how a farm operation works, Mr. Speaker, just as the member for Regina-Wascana would have seen how a farm operation works. You harvest your crop, you put it in the bin, and then you move it to the elevator for sale. It is at the elevator that the crop gets purchased. When the crop is sitting in the bin and the elevator is full, the farmer cannot move the crop from the bin to the elevator. Therefore it sits there. The farmer's bills are adding up because the people he borrowed money from during the summer in order to get the crop in and harvested cannot now be paid.
With this bill the government is adding an extra burden to this whole process of trying to move the grain from the bin to the elevator to export and as such is throwing a damper on the whole orderly marketing of grain.
Under no circumstances can the motion moved by the member for Regina-Wascana be heard at this point in time. The government still has not heard from a number of rural representatives both of my party and of the Official Opposition in the House. A number of witnesses are anxious, the Prairie Pools included, to appear before the committee of the House.
The Prairie Pools wants this government to hold off any planned changes to the cash advance until there is a thorough study of the possible effects of farm cash flow on agricultural marketing, which means there is a normal course of delay that should be taking place here.
If this government were really serious about protecting the interests of western Canadian farmers, it would withdraw this bill immediately and put into place the provisions of the statutes which presently exist. Those statutes call for the government simply to put out the forms for the cash advance program so that the farm community would, right now, have access to the cash advance. Interest-free as it may be, that is exactly the way it should be.

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
I also want to point out that I have received a number of phone calls over the course of the last couple of weeks from producers, some of whom are being pressured to pay debts by the Farm Credit Corporation which is stating: "If you can get a cash advance, we will be able to swing you through until this whole process is complete." Those particular farmers are wondering what they are supposed to do.
The government, last April 27, knew what it wanted to do with this cash advance program. It sat on it all the way through to now, and some of my constituents are in a real bind because they are not able to get the cash advance on which they are counting to pay off their debts. It is a direct responsibility of this government to ensure that farmers are able to hang on to what they have come to count on. In fact farmers do count on it for the sale of their grain and the maintenance of their farms.
This government has been so proud of its record on agriculture. Every time somebody on the other side of the House stands up, it is to talk about what this government has done for agriculture.
What state is agriculture in in this country? It is worse than it was under the previous government which had also mowed agriculture into the ground. Everything this government has done has been simply band-aids on problems. Not a single financial problem in the agricultural sector has been alleviated by any of the programs that have been instituted since 1984. One full term in government, and now we are into a second term of this particular government and the farm crisis is broadening. Bills like this are creating no end of difficulty for the producers who do not know what to do from one day to the next. They do not know where they are going to turn.
This year the crop in some parts of Saskatchewan and western Canada is better than it was last year because of the massive drought that hit the prairie provinces. There is a bit better crop in some areas of Saskatchewan and western Canada, and what happens? They cannot sell it now. They cannot get the money for the crop now
because this government is holding back on this whole interest-free cash advance program.
The whole process up to this point has been quite disgusting and unnerving. The government should actually be ashamed of itself for talking about how wonderful it has been to agriculture, and then on the other hand pushing it down one more time. Not only is the government going to have a tax revolt on its hands and a train revolt, it is going to have an agriculture revolt if it keeps this sort of thing up.
The last time I spoke on this bill was on the motion of the Liberal party to hoist this matter for six months. At that point I suggested that the government was listening as much on this issue as it was listening on the issues of the goods and services tax and of VIA Rail. We have a situation where the people of Canada, the producers, the people who are most affected by government legislation, are doing the talking and the government is not doing the listening. They are doing exactly the opposite thing of what is demanded by the market-place, the market that they are so proud of out there.
I have had a large number of telephone calls in my riding concerning the cash advance. Every single one of those calls advocates a support for the interest-free cash advance, not because they are looking for a hand-out from the government and free money, but because that is the nature of this program. That is what is needed. A short time ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre outlined the purpose of this whole process when he stated:
The Advance Payments for Crops Act was a benefit not only to producers but to small businesses as well. As we all know, the farmer lives on credit for a good portion of the year and advance payments allow him to pay his bills to small business people who are themselves suffering.
As this government will know, the hon. member who chairs the goods and services tax committee, the finance committee here in the House, has heard from people all over Canada. Small business people in western Canada are saying that this government, through the goods and services tax, is putting a burden on them that they cannot bear.
One of the reasons they cannot bear it is the pressure from the agricultural community at this point that the bills are not being paid. The economy is just too poor.
My colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, also stated:
With this change in the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, it is quite clear that farmers will not be utilizing the programs as they had
October 24, 1989

before. A study by the UPA in Quebec indicated that approximately 10 per cent of producers now utilizing the Advance Payments for Crops Act will utilize it when the interests amended are added to this act.
It is destroying the program. Putting the interest rate on to this program simply eliminates it, simply gets rid of the program altogether. This government may just as well have reduced and destroyed the program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed myself last Friday when I was speaking to the amendment on this bill. I was only allowed 20 minutes and I have two hours' worth of stuff.
I want to start off by mentioning my hon. friend, the member for Regina-Wascana, who did what I consider to be the dumbest thing any member from the prairies could ever do, that is, to try and cut off debate on interest-free cash advances for farmers. I am not complaining about that. If he is going to be that stupid, I will be glad to help him out.
I want to say to my hon. friend that I challenge him to debate this matter in some place in his riding like Montmartre. You set the date, time, and place, and I will be there. I want you to do that; just give me a couple of weeks' notice. We will take this out to your farmers in the rural part of Regina-Wascana. Of course one of us will bring the Hansard record with us.
The government is breaking its own law by refusing both Treasury Board and cabinet to authorize the Canadian Wheat Board or the other agencies in the rest of Canada to issue cash advances, interest-free, on farm production.
I hope there are some legal eagles checking on this because I suspect the law says the Minister of Finance "shall", not "may" pay to provide the funds for the Canadian Wheat Board and the other agencies that issue the funds as a cash advance on that farm production.
If there ever was a backhanded, underhanded manner in which to subvert the law of the land, it is to not provide the money. The new crop year starts August 1 in the case of grain in the Canadian Wheat Board area.

October 24, 1989
Government Orders
Since August 1, the government has refused to allow the Canadian Wheat Board to issue cash advances which under the law it is allowed to do. What lengths the government goes to to subvert the law.
It is the same as what Otto Lang did when he tried to repeal the temporary Wheat Reserves Act to save the government $100 million by not having paid the Canadian Wheat Board storage costs on certain amounts of grain for the previous 18 months. We took him to court and beat him. We collected $100 million for the grain producers of western Canada.
The same thing is occurring again, only this time the faces have changed. They are just as ugly as the previous ones. The names have changed, Liberal-Conservative, Conservative-Liberal, the same breed of cats. Now the Tories are doing the same damn thing that they condemned the Liberals for doing.
When we are talking about interest-free, I had a chance to briefly mention last Friday about deferred corporation taxes. Almost $40 billion have accrued on the books of this country by corporations that were allowed to defer their taxes and they do not pay them back. In fact, it is an interest-free loan.
I suggested last Friday, Mr. Speaker, that if you were to charge 10 per cent interest on those deferred corporation taxes, which is at least 3 per cent below the bank rate, you would pick up $4 billion a year for the Government of Canada. I think that is a neat way to reduce the deficit.
The point is, there can be interest-free loans for corporations like the CPR, Bell Telephone, and International Nickel, but an interest-free cash advance for farmers is a no-no, say the Tories.
I do not necessarily know whether or not there will be any resurrections, but if there were one I would hope it would be the former member for Prince Albert who would come back and haunt the hon. Minister of Energy who sits there as a fine Christian gentleman. Mr. Diefenbaker, I am sure, would love to shake his jowls at him, poke his finger in his ear, in his nose, and in his eye about what he is doing to a program brought in in 1957.1 find this passing strange. In fact, in western Canada, people of all political stripes applauded Mr. Diefenbaker, his political foes as well as his friends, and every farm organization, for bringing in something that we had been
tiying to get the Liberals to do since 1947, and we got it in 1957.
Who is trying to do away with it? The same outfit that brought it in. I do not think even the Liberals are that stupid, but the Tories are. In fact, they are setting records all the time. They set one today.
Many times the Tories berated the Liberals when they were in government for closure and time allocation and they did a terrible number of them. When one is in, the other one is out and all they do is exchange speeches. But the Tories today set a record. Always before, with the Liberals, you had a least two or three days to debate, but today the Tories set a record of one day. How about that? What a record to meet.
Now the Tories have set another record. They are destroying a program that was unanimously approved of, accepted, agreed to, and supported right across political lines and by all the farm organizations, including the ones that fight among themselves and with each other, and has been supported consistently since 1957.
I know it is a fond hope, but if the three and a half Tories who are in here would not mind, if they would go back to their own caucus and their-

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE SAFEGUARD LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY AN ACT TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION AS A CORPORATION UNDER THE LAWS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
that Bill S-5, an Act to authorize the Safeguard Life Assurance Company to be continued as a corporation under the laws of the Province of Quebec, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the member for Levis, the city where a former parliamentary stenographer and editor for the House of Commons from 1892 to 1917, Alphonse Desjardins, founded Canada's first caisse populate, the first of 1,343 Desjardins caisses populaires and credit unions in Quebec, I have the honour to table today a Bill to authorize the Safeguard Life Assurance Company to be continued under Quebec's Insurance Act.
On June 29, 1989, the Senate approved this bill on third reading. Established in 1901, the Safeguard was the first insurance company created and financed by the French-speaking business community in Canada. This share company again made economic history in our country in 1962 by becoming the exclusive property of the Caisses populaires Desjardins of Quebec, that is, 100
Private Members' Business
per cent owned by them. The Safeguard was the instrument-some would say the turning point-for bringing together the first holding company in Quebec for financial institutions that belong to our fellow citizens through some 1,343 caisses populaires and credit unions in Quebec that make up the Desjardins Movement.
After a modest beginning, the Safeguard could take pride in being the largest French-speaking life insurance company in Canada in 1962, with $52 million in assets. Today, the Safeguard has $800 million in assets.
In March 1988, the elected directors of the Desjardins Movement approved the plan for the growth and capitalization of the Safeguard. Accordingly, Desjardins has already increased the company's capital and made a commitment to its future capitalization.
Today, the Safeguard is asking to be continued under Quebec jurisdiction. This is what the customers, shareholders and managers of the Safeguard want so that it can prosper and grow in this highly competitive and fast-changing environment in our country. To do so, it needs to be governed by a single control and supervision authority, the same one that already regulates all the other activities of the Desjardins Movement, namely the Inspector General of Financial Institutions of Quebec.
In addition, then-Minister of State for Finance, Thomas Hockin, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, Mr. Mackenzie, and the Inspector General of Financial Institutions of Quebec, Mr. Bouchard, were informed of all the details of the Safeguard's plan and gave their support to this Bill.
As I said earlier, the Senate studied and approved this bill before the summer break. There was no opposition to this bill when it was considered in the Senate committee.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of continuing this company under Quebec jurisdiction is not to escape from or reduce supervision of its affairs but to achieve greater openness.
Indeed, such a move will force the company, in addition to satisfying the rules governing federally incorporated insurance companies and the rules set by Quebec, to meet all the requirements in all Canadian

October 24, 1989
Private Members' Business
provinces from which federally chartered companies are exempt.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the proposed transfer of jurisdiction for the Safeguard makes a great deal of sense and is clearly to the benefit of its shareholders and customers and the public at large. Therefore, I urge the members of this House to pass the Safeguard bill quickly so that this company can carry out its planned transfer of jurisdiction as soon as possible.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE SAFEGUARD LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY AN ACT TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION AS A CORPORATION UNDER THE LAWS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking today to Bill S-5, an act to authorize the Safeguard Life Assurance Company to be continued as a corporation under the laws of the province of Quebec. I am supporting the motion that it be referred to a legislative committee.

On the other hand, it is important that we look veiy carefully at the reasons for the transfer of this company and that it not be because perhaps under the Quebec charter there might be considerably more loopholes of which they can take advantage. I support the motion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE SAFEGUARD LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY AN ACT TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION AS A CORPORATION UNDER THE LAWS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the debate on Bill S-5 to authorize the Safeguard Life Assurance Company to be continued as a corporation under the laws of the province of Quebec.

The office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions told the company that they would not raise objections if the company were to show that such a move was endorsed by shareholders and policyholders alike.
This position was then confirmed by the minister responsible for financial institutions because it was in keeping with the guidelines followed in recent years.
During the next few months the management of Safeguard consulted with their policyholders and shareholders, 95 per cent of whom approved the project aimed at securing a provincial charter. This is why the office of the Superintendent has since confirmed that it has no objection to Safeguard acquiring a provincial charter.
The bill now under consideration would authorize Safeguard to substitute a Quebec government charter for the charter it now has.
As my colleague from Levis (Mr. Fontaine) pointed out, the bill was passed by the Senate after committee hearings where it heard evidence from company management.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should-and the opposition agrees-refer Bill S-5 to a legislative committee for further consultation and disposition.

FISHERIES-FISH PROCESSING REGULATIONS/ENFORCEMENT OF LANDING REQUIREMENTS
['The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 24 (1).']

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, in discussing the final report of the free trade panel, the Minister for International Trade said, in effect, although I did not take his words down accurately, that compensation is not easy to calculate, but the ruling is being considered. These are the words that interest me most: "Whatever we do will be in the interest of Canadians generally and those involved in the industry in particular".
I fear that the people involved in the fishing industry in British Columbia will take very little comfort from those words, because they have been hearing similar comments from ministers on the government side for some years now.
In November, 1987, when the Minister of Fisheries was asked about the effect of the GATT ruling, he made it quite clear as to what the government position was. He offered his assurances that those jobs would not be jeopardized in any way. He went on to state:
The provisions of Canada's participation in GATT allow for export controls for the purpose of preserving security of supply, for ensuring adequacy of supply to plants and for the conservation of the resource. Many member nations of GATT take advantage of such export restrictions.
Later on he said, "-a government which spends over $100 million a year to manage and enhance the west coast salmon and herring industry will not allow jobs, historically established, to be threatened by any such initiative."
Further on he stated, "What we have is a panel recommendation which will, in all likelihood, be overturned by the GATT council of which we are a member, and we will be opposing that recommendation when it
Adjournment Debate
reaches the GATT council." Those are very comforting words from almost two years ago. But the government took no such action. It had the report from GATT, and an opportunity to appeal it. It chose not to appeal. It had the opportunity to take alternative actions, and it chose not to do that.
The government did nothing in fact, and then it signed its way into the free trade agreement, or at least accepted the final wording of the free trade deal on December 10, 1987, in which agreement it agreed not to go against any GATT decision.
On March 21, 1988, the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister for International Trade announced that Canada would not veto the GATT panel ruling. It had that opportunity and they chose not to do that. It had an opportunity to impose export taxes, prior to the free trade agreement being signed. It chose not to do that. The next day, the full GATT council accepted the panel ruling.
Then the government came up with alternative proposals. It had some sure fire methods of controlling the situation. They could have vetoed the GATT council decision. It could have imposed an export tax. It chose not to do either. Instead, totally ignoring the recommendations from everyone involved in the fishing industry in the west coast, it brought in a new system of regulations, landing requirements for B.C. salmon and herring. This was going to be the way of saving the industry for British Columbia.
A panel was set up in response to the Americans raising this issue again. The panel brought in a preliminary report on September 15. That is almost 40 days ago now. The preliminary report, which has not been released to this date to the best of my knowledge, although we were able to get copies of it from the Americans, ruled against Canada.
There was a suggestion within the body of the report that if we did not insist on 100 per cent landing, then it might be okay. It did not state it would be, but stated it might be okay if we had something less than 100 per cent insistence of landing in British Columbia. The government has taken a lot of comfort from the fact that the panel, in the body of its report, suggested that something less than 100 per cent might be satisfactory. It did not state that it would be.
Once again, as I say, the government has taken comfort from that statement. But it has not told the fishing industry, the people involved in the processing

October 24, 1989
Adjournment Debate
industry, or the fishermen themselves, just what position the government intends to take.
It had 61 days in total from the release of the preliminary report. It has 21 days left, and it has chosen not to say anything, other than that it will consult the fishing industry. Again, I have not been able to find out from anyone in the fishing industry that the government is consulting anyone, and the days are slipping by.
Canada did react to the preliminary report. It had a position paper. But there is no rehearing of the case, although there was an opportunity given the death of one of the members of the panel and his replacement. There was an opportunity to have a rehearing and to hear new evidence. Evidence was available. Canada had the evidence. It has it in this paper which goes into the details as to what extent exports were going on in spite of the landing regulations. The fish were being landed in British Columbia and millions of pounds of fish were being shipped out after they were landed. So it is obvious from the evidence from affidavits that are sworn by Mr. Nordlandmann, the manager of the largest shipper of unprocessed salmon from B.C. landing stations. The evidence was there to show that it did not interfere with the shipments to the United States. Canada should have won that case. Canada still has the opportunity to say, "We are going to insist on 100 per cent landing because we need it to control the resource".

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada and the United States received the final report of the FTA panel on Pacific salmon and herring on October 16 of this year. We are currently reviewing the report and its impact on Canadian landing requirements for Pacific salmon and herring and have not yet come to a decision. We have begun to consult with the B.C. government and the industry and have received some useful suggestions.
Under FTA rules, Canada and the United States must reach a decision on this case within 30 days of receipt of the final report. Regardless of the final decision, Canada will ensure that the conservation and management of the salmon and herring resource will not be compromised. The panel has recognized that it is the sovereign right of Canada to collect conservation and management information and that Canada does not have to depend on a foreign nation for that information.
The panel stated that Canada's landing requirements would be acceptable if provision was made to exempt from landing that portion of the catch whose exportation without landing would not impede the data collection process. The report also stated that the actual proportion should be determined on the basis of the actual data and management needs of each fishery or group of fisheries, but that a 10 to 20 per cent level would provide appropriate guidance.
The government feels strongly that it must take time to carefully study the report and complete consultations with the province of British Columbia and the industry before publicly announcing its purpose.
The government recognizes that it takes time to provide a proper assessment of the implications of the report. The critical question is whether the report permits a realistic achievement of our conservation and management requirements; that is, the ability to perform statistically valid biological sampling, the ability to obtain information needed for effective in-season management and the ability to validate catch by species, number and weight, area and time.
With the above in mind, the government is hopeful that through the consultative process and taking the time necessary to measure the impacts on the conservation of these essential resources, we will be able to ensure that our goals are met.

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ACT-DISABLED PERSONS
CANADA PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ACT-DISABLED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to again raise in this House a concern that I have relative to the Canada Pension Plan disability pension provisions. This flows from a question put to the Minister of National Health and Welfare back on June 14,1989, a statement pursuant to standing order of approximately the same date, and also a question put back in May 1988.
The concern relates to those Canadians who have paid into the Canada Pension Plan over the years who become disabled and, as a result of the disability, have to leave their employment, but who are delayed in applying for their disability pension. These are not common occurrences nowadays because most Canadians are
October 24, 1989

aware of the opportunity for disability pension. Indeed, if they are not, I am sure that the availability is brought to their attention by others.
But there are situations, and I think particularly of a Mrs. Donna Sinclair of Swift Current, Saskatchewan, a constituent of mine, with whose case I am well familiar. This is a lady who is 60 years old at this point in time, who contributed to the Canada Pension Plan, I believe, in 11 of 13 years between 1966 and 1978 or 1979. She had to leave her employment as a result of diabetes and subsequently has had both legs amputated. Somehow she did not know or did not understand that there was a possibility of a Canada Pension Plan disability pension. She finally learned of it from a friend or from relatives and applied in 1987. Of course, when she applied, she learned that she did not meet the test of recency because in order to be eligible, a person must have contributed, I believe, in five of the last ten years, in her particular situation. So she did not qualify.
It seems to me just and fair that people in this situation who have contributed through their employment, who have had to leave that employment through disability and who simply did not know of the availability, nonetheless ought not to be precluded from receiving a disability pension. Obviously there is not a simple answer to this because it does, I believe, require an amendment to the legislation. I think it is probably more complicated because the minister does not just wave a wand and do this. I think it requires federal-provincial co-operation and I am sure a lot of other things enter into it.
At this point in time, I certainly am not intending to be critical of the minister who, I think, is a very able and articulate individual. However, I do have a concern in this case that not enough is being done. I do not think that the answer given to me back in June is satisfactory, the answer being that I should put a motion on the Order Paper in regard to Private Members' Business and if and when that comes up the matter will again be raised.
We all know how Private Members' Business works. The matter may never be drawn. It is a matter of the luck of the draw and so I am taking the opportunity to again
Adjournment Debate
bring the matter to the attention of members in this House.
Mrs. Sinclair is not alone. I know of another situation in my constituency and other members from all sides have raised the matter with me as well. It is evident that in every constituency there are two or three or four such individuals. So it is not just an isolated situation. I think it is a situation that is deserving of attention and I, therefore, again express to the minister and to the department that it would be well to try to find a solution to accommodate people like Mrs. Sinclair who, I think, have played by all of the rules but did not understand that there was an availability.
I think what we are seeking here today is a review of the situation. I must compliment my colleague, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Human Rights and Disabled Persons, because he has responded and indicated that that committee will be examining certain aspects of the Canada Pension Plan and has undertaken to study the economic factors involved in integrating disabled persons into our society. If and when that comes forward, certainly we will be making representations to him and his committee. I thank him for his interest in the matter.
I think this is one problem which really does need the attention of both levels of government, that is, the federal government and the provinces. I sincerely hope that at some time in the not too distant future, the matter can become the subject of some discussion between those levels of government in regard to opening up the Canada Pension Plan legislation.
In closing, I appreciate the responses that I received of some caring and some compassion and some concern and, above all else, a willingness on the part of government to try to do something about this situation. There are people who are deserving, who are needy, and I think they need some kind of response.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ACT-DISABLED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the concerns of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia with regard to the recency test which is applied to Canada Pension Plan disability benefit applicants.

October 24, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Disability benefits are intended to replace earnings lost through disability. Therefore, a recent attachment to the workforce was a requirement for benefit eligibility. This government has already amended the recency test by providing more flexible eligibility requirements.
Under Bill C-116 effective January, 1987, the Canada Pension Plan disability provisions were amended so that persons who have contributed to the CPP in two of the last three years, or five of the last ten years prior to their application, can meet the contributory requirements.
Prior to the passage of this legislation, the test of recency required that contributions were made in five of the last ten years and one-third of the contributory period.
It may also be noted that under Bill C-116, the time limit of 12 months retroactively for the determination of disability in the original act was extended to 15 months in 1987. Through this amendment, some persons may qualify for disability benefits up to six years or more after they leave work. Most private insurance plans for disability have much more stringent recency tests. Most limit their protection to between 30 and 90 days following the cessation of work.
I wish to say that the hon. member is not alone in his concern for the disabled Canadians who failed to meet the CPP recency tests. The department is currently reviewing the limit on retroactivity determination to see whether some further extension of this time limit would be feasible.
However, the hon. member should be cognizant of the fact that amendments to this effect must be undertaken with caution, given the possibility that they could cause more problems than they solve. For example, the farther we go in the past, the more difficult it is to assess precisely when all the relevant medical and socioeconomic factors may have resulted in the disability of the individual. This is because the factors contributing to the disability often change over time. Indeed, such changes may lead to the amelioration, the elimination, or the degeneration of the health condition.
Furthermore, if the retroactive period were substantially extended the process of disability determination would likely require more information and resources from the client, and they would likely increase the time spent on disability adjudication, potentially delaying the initial payments for some individuals. Consequently, we have to ensure that the current administrative structure can respond adequately and efficiently to any change in the legislation.
In light of these and other conditions, the feasibility of a legislative amendment must be thoroughly evaluated. At the present time, the government does not have a specific time frame within which it intends to reopen the CPP act. The hon. member knows that his request to open the act to make amendments involves a process which is complex and requires considerable time. Major changes to the CPP require the approval of two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the Canadian population, as well as the approval of Parliament.
However, I assure the hon. member that should the act be reopened, his recommendations will be taken into consideration.
CANADA POST CORPORATION-SERVICES IN COMMUNITIES/MINISTER'S POSITION

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ACT-DISABLED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity tonight to address the question which I asked in this House on June 15. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was on that date that Canada Post announced its profit of $96 million. It was on that day that a number of members rose in the House of Commons to discuss that profit and what it means to the services for residents of Canada.
As a result of the profit shown by Canada Post Corporation, and other matters, the Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations Committee has embarked upon a study of the operations of Canada Post, and by this time next week will have begun the hearings across Canada into the operations of Canada Post and a discussion about the future and the opportunities that Canada Post gives to residents of Canada.
The question I was asking of the minister concerned the communities from coast to coast in Canada that are organizing to save their rural post offices, or get door-to-door delivery. They are being denied the opportunity
October 24, 1989

to do that, at the same time that Canada Post records a profit of $96 million.
Canada Post, the federal government, and the minister responsible for Canada Post, made a clear choice when they decided to accept the profits of $96 million over the needs of the rural communities of Canada and the service requirements of the people who live there. Canada Post and the federal government chose big business over Canadian people in providing that service.
Canada Post should take that profit of $96 million and use it to repair some of the damage that it has done to the postal system over the last few years. The federal government should insist that this money be used to extend door-to-door delivery service to suburban residents. The government should insist this capital be used to re-open rural post offices which have been shut across Canada.
Canada Post should be seen first and foremost not as a money machine for the federal government, but to honour its mandate which is service first. The government has turned Canada Post into a Frankenstein of Crown corporations, and it is running amok, not accountable to Parliament, to the committees or to the people of Canada.
At the time, I also released a ten-point plan which I thought should govern the future operations of Canada Post. I would like to put part of that on the record tonight in the time allotted to me. The ten-point program includes: The primary goal of Canada Post should be to provide and extend service to Canadians. The profit created by Canada Post should be directly rolled back into maintaining and expanding service to Canadians; that all 167 rural post offices closed by Canada Post should be immediately re-opened, and that the government should review rural postal operations with the goal of extending service to areas currently in need of service.
The federal government should ensure that door-to-door delivery is extended to suburban residents, and it should do away with the supermailboxes which have become super headaches across the country. Canada Post's campaign of harassment and intimidation of its workers must be halted, and the Canada Post Crown corporation should be expected to be a model employer
Adjournment Debate
that sees the link between good working conditions, harmonious labour relations, and the provision of better postal service to Canadians. All post office operations should be contracted in and a halt should be put on further erosion of service and working conditions through contracting out. Service should be extended where warranted at post offices to include the sale of paper, tape or other related items for the use in preparing parcels for mailing.
The Government of Canada and Canada Post should examine the possibility of providing services to Canadians which are provided in other countries, such as, flower sales and dry cleaning drop-off points in rural parts of Canada. The Government of Canada and Canada Post should abandon the plans to sell off parts of the postal system to the private sector and get back to the business of providing service to Canadians. Finally, the Rural Route Mail Carriers Organization should be recognized by the government so that it can negotiate working conditions and standards that it does not currently have.
In presenting that ten-point program, I reiterate my previous call from the spring sitting of this Parliament for a public inquiry into the Post Office, a public inquiry which comes from the Government of Canada as opposed to the Consumers and Corporate Affairs Commission. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, during Question Period I called on the minister to institute a moratorium on the conversion and closing of rural post offices until such time as the committee has reported and Parliament has a chance to read the report.
Canada Post's expenditure earlier this year on 64,000 videos for employees, a new mega wardrobe for its employees, its campaign to take the Canada out of Canada Post, and its national coloured glossy promotional leaflet are clear signals to Canadians: the federal government and Canada Post are trying their hardest to make our postal system a pretty package for the private sector to facilitate the government's plans to privatize Canada Post and roll back the clock on postal service and working conditions.

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF ACT-DISABLED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1981 when the post office was incorporated into a Crown Corporation, it was mandated to improve the service and become financially self-sufficient.

Adjournment Debate
This year is an important milestone for the post office regarding these objectives. Canada Post Corporation recorded a profit of $96 million. It is the first time in 30 years that the people of Canada are not required to subsidize their postal service when they pay their taxes.
The hon. member has suggested that the minister responsible for Canada Post is taking liberties with the mandate given to the corporation by Parliament. As well, he is suggesting that the profits have been achieved at the expense of service. It is an interesting suggestion but, unfortunately for the hon. member, it does not withstand close scrutiny.
When the post office was transformed into a Crown corporation, it was given an asset base that was in great need of attention. Capital investment levels were not sufficient at the time to maintain its base. Over the next five years, the corporation plans to invest $2.5 billion in new equipment and machinery. This investment is fundamental if the corporation is to continue to provide a postal service that is marked by being accessible, reliable and affordable. These investments will benefit all the customers of Canada Post and are only possible so long as the corporation continues to make a profit. Otherwise, we will return to the days when Canada Post was having to be a drain on the national treasury.
The corporation's achievement of being self-sufficient has not been achieved at the expense of service. On the contrary, the service that is provided by Canada Post has been improving. Today, the accounting firm of Ernst-Young, formerly Clarkson Gordon, released its service performance report on Canada Post. This report demonstrates that once again the corporation is meeting its commitment of on time delivery. The report reveals that the rate of on time delivery for a properly prepared,
first-class letter mailed within the same urban area was 96 per cent. For delivery in the same province, it was also 96 per cent. Between provinces, these figures were 97 per cent. So you can see that we are getting on time delivery between urban centres. We have been getting on time delivery within the provinces and we are getting on time delivery between provinces. That is quite impressive for a corporation that delivers 33 million pieces of mail a day to nearly 10.7 million addresses.
Not only are delivery standards being met, but the corporation is working hard on improving accessibility. The corporation intends to increase the number of places that customers can access postal products and service. The corporation has made a commitment to Canadians that will keep rate increases below the price of inflation. This promise is being kept, as seen with the present proposed rate increase that is now before the Postal Service Review Committee.
The corporation has put forward a request to raise the price of a first-class stamp by one cent. This amounts to a 2.6 per cent increase. This is what is meant by self-sufficiency while improving service. I, and many others, do not think that that is wrong, but rather that it is something that should be encouraged and something that we are very proud of. We wish the post office continued success.
In conclusion, it is really nice to stand in the House of Commons with the galleries overflowing, the Speaker in his chair and the crowds cheering. It is wonderful to be here.
